authoredSolutions.31: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent) condenses with a carbonyl group to give an orange-yellow 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone precipitate. Of the four choices only the aldehyde carries a \(>C=O\) group, so only it can form the hydrazone. Halogens, ethers and amines have no carbonyl carbon and give no precipitate. Hence the correct option is (A) aldehyde.
authoredSolutions.32: 4-Methoxybenzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, so with HCHO/NaOH it undergoes a crossed Cannizzaro reaction and is reduced to 4-methoxybenzyl alcohol (formaldehyde is oxidised to formate). NaH then deprotonates this alcohol and \(CH_{3}CH_{2}Br\) alkylates it (Williamson synthesis) to the ethyl benzyl ether. Hot HI cleaves both ethers: the aryl methyl ether gives the phenol \(+\ CH_{3}I\), while the benzylic C-O bond is cleaved at the benzylic carbon to give the benzyl iodide. Product \(A\) is therefore 4-hydroxybenzyl iodide, which is the structure shown in option (C).
authoredSolutions.33: Adding \(FeCl_{3}\) to excess hot water hydrolyses it to a sol of hydrated ferric oxide, \(Fe_{2}O_{3}\cdot xH_{2}O\). By the Fajans adsorption rule the dispersed particles preferentially adsorb the common ion \(Fe^{3+}\) present in the medium. This gives the colloidal particles a fixed positive charge (the classic positively charged ferric hydroxide sol). Hence the charge is (A) positive.
authoredSolutions.34: The four schemes in List-I are: (A) \(C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}\) with \(Cu_{2}Cl_{2}\) giving chlorobenzene, which is the Sandmeyer reaction (ii); (B) the same diazonium salt with \(Cu/HCl\), which is the Gattermann reaction (iv); (C) \(2CH_{3}CH_{2}Cl + 2Na\) in dry ether giving \(n\)-butane, the Wurtz reaction (i); and (D) an aryl halide with \(Na\) in dry ether giving biphenyl, the Fittig reaction (iii). Note that Sandmeyer uses cuprous halide while Gattermann uses copper powder with the halogen acid, which is the only difference between (A) and (B). The matching is therefore (A)-(ii), (B)-(iv), (C)-(i), (D)-(iii), i.e. option (C).
authoredSolutions.35: In \(CH_{2}=C=CH-CH_{3}\), \(C_{1}\) is a doubly bonded terminal carbon with three \(\sigma\) bonds, hence \(sp^{2}\). \(C_{2}\) is the central allenic carbon carrying two double bonds and only two \(\sigma\) bonds, so it is \(sp\) hybridised and makes the two \(\pi\) systems mutually perpendicular. \(C_{3}\) has one double bond and three \(\sigma\) bonds, so it is \(sp^{2}\), and \(C_{4}\) of the methyl group has four \(\sigma\) bonds, so it is \(sp^{3}\). The order is \(sp^{2}, sp, sp^{2}, sp^{3}\), which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.36: Sucrose is a non-reducing disaccharide built from \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-fructose joined through both anomeric carbons, so (A) matches (ii). Lactose (milk sugar) is made of \(\beta\)-D-galactose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose linked \(\beta(1\rightarrow 4)\), so (B) matches (i). Maltose consists of two \(\alpha\)-D-glucose units linked \(\alpha(1\rightarrow 4)\), so (C) matches (iii). The correct matching (A)-(ii), (B)-(i), (C)-(iii) is option (D).
authoredSolutions.37: Oxides of non-metals are acidic, oxides of metals are generally basic, and \(N_{2}O\) is a neutral oxide. In option (A) \(N_{2}O\) is neutral and \(BaO\) basic; in (B) \(CaO\) is basic; in (C) \(CaO\) is again basic, so none of these is a wholly acidic pair. Only \(B_{2}O_{3}\) and \(SiO_{2}\) are both non-metal oxides that dissolve in alkali to give borate and silicate. Hence the acidic pair is option (D).
authoredSolutions.38: Calgon is sodium hexametaphosphate, \(Na_{6}P_{6}O_{18}\), written as \(Na_{2}[Na_{4}(PO_{3})_{6}]\); it is also called Graham's salt, is polymeric and water soluble, and removes \(Ca^{2+}\) and \(Mg^{2+}\) by forming soluble complex anions rather than by precipitation. So statements (B), (C) and (D) are all true. The abundance order in the earth's crust is \(O > Si > Al > Fe > Ca > Na > Mg > K\), so the second most abundant element is silicon, which calgon does not contain. The statement that is NOT true is therefore option (A).
authoredSolutions.39: Ceric ammonium nitrate reacts with an alcoholic \(-OH\) group to give a red colouration, so it is the standard test for alcohols. Chloroform with alcoholic \(KOH\) generates dichlorocarbene, which converts a primary amine into a foul-smelling isocyanide (the carbylamine test), so it identifies primary amines. Phenols would answer to neutral \(FeCl_{3}\), not to either of these reagents. Hence the two reagents identify alcohol and amine respectively, option (A).
authoredSolutions.40: \(TlI_{3}\) is not a \(Tl(III)\) iodide but \(Tl^{+}(I_{3})^{-}\), isomorphous with \(Cs^{+}(I_{3})^{-}\), so the metal is indeed in the \(+1\) state and Assertion A is correct. The electronic configuration of thallium is \([Xe]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^{2}6p^{1}\), so it does carry fourteen \(f\) electrons and Reason R is also a correct statement. However the preference for \(+1\) arises from the inert pair effect, i.e. the reluctance of the \(6s^{2}\) pair to participate in bonding, not from the mere count of \(f\) electrons. Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A, which is option (C).
authoredSolutions.41: Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes less negative down a group, which would predict \(O > S > Se > Te\). Oxygen breaks this trend because its \(2p\) subshell is unusually compact, so the incoming electron suffers strong inter-electronic repulsion and oxygen releases less energy than sulphur. The magnitudes are roughly \(S(-200) > Se(-195) > Te(-190) > O(-141)\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\), so sulphur has the most negative value and oxygen falls below tellurium. The correct order is \(S > Se > Te > O\), option (A).
authoredSolutions.42: The substrate carries two \(-CH_{2}CH_{2}CHO\) chains on adjacent ring carbons, and dilute NaOH generates the enolate at the \(\alpha\)-carbon of one chain. That enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of the other chain intramolecularly; counting the two aromatic carbons, the two \(\alpha\)-carbons, the two \(\beta\)-carbons and the attacked carbonyl carbon gives a seven-membered ring fused to the benzene ring. Heating then dehydrates the aldol to the conjugated \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated aldehyde. Product \(A\) is thus the benzo-fused seven-membered ring bearing a \(C=C\) conjugated to a \(-CHO\) group, which is option (A); option (D) would be the Cannizzaro product, which cannot form here since both aldehydes have \(\alpha\)-hydrogens.
authoredSolutions.43: Siderite is \(FeCO_{3}\), an iron ore, so (A) matches (iii). Calamine is \(ZnCO_{3}\), so (B) matches (v). Malachite is the basic copper carbonate \(CuCO_{3}\cdot Cu(OH)_{2}\), so (C) matches (i). Cryolite is \(Na_{3}AlF_{6}\), used as a flux in aluminium extraction, so (D) matches (iv). The correct matching (A)-(iii), (B)-(v), (C)-(i), (D)-(iv) is option (B).
authoredSolutions.44: \(SOCl_{2}\) converts an alcoholic \(-OH\) into \(-Cl\), but a phenolic \(-OH\) does not react because the C-O bond has partial double-bond character from lone-pair delocalisation into the ring. The substrate has three hydroxyl groups: a phenolic \(-OH\) on the aromatic ring, a secondary alcoholic \(-OH\) on the saturated ring, and a primary benzylic \(-CH_{2}OH\). Both alcoholic groups are therefore replaced by chlorine while the phenolic \(-OH\) survives unchanged. Product \(A\) retains the phenol and carries \(-CHCl-\) and \(-CH_{2}Cl\), which is option (B); option (D), in which even the phenolic \(-OH\) is replaced, is wrong for exactly this reason.
authoredSolutions.45: Sodium carbonate is manufactured by the Solvay (ammonia-soda) process, so (A) matches (iv). Titanium is purified by the Van Arkel vapour-phase method through \(TiI_{4}\), so (B) matches (iii). Chlorine is obtained industrially by the Deacon process, the catalytic air oxidation of \(HCl\) over \(CuCl_{2}\), so (C) matches (i). Sodium hydroxide is made by electrolysis of brine in the Castner-Kellner mercury-cathode cell, so (D) matches (ii). The correct matching (A)-(iv), (B)-(iii), (C)-(i), (D)-(ii) is option (B).
authoredSolutions.46: Bond order in molecular orbital theory is \(\frac{1}{2}(N_{b}-N_{a})\). For \(Ne_{2}\) every bonding orbital is matched by a filled antibonding orbital, giving bond order \(0\), so (A) matches (iii) and \(Ne_{2}\) does not exist. \(N_{2}\) has \(10\) bonding and \(4\) antibonding electrons, giving bond order \(3\), so (B) matches (iv). \(F_{2}\) has bond order \(1\) and \(O_{2}\) has bond order \(2\), so (C) matches (i) and (D) matches (ii). The correct matching (A)-(iii), (B)-(iv), (C)-(i), (D)-(ii) is option (A).
authoredSolutions.47: Protium \(^{1}_{1}H\) and deuterium \(^{2}_{1}H\) are stable isotopes and the proton \(H^{+}\) is simply a bare nucleus, so none of these is radioactive. Tritium \(^{3}_{1}H\) has two neutrons for one proton, and this high \(n/p\) ratio makes the nucleus unstable. It decays by \(\beta^{-}\) emission to \(^{3}_{2}He\) with a half-life of about \(12.3\) years, releasing unusually low-energy \(\beta^{-}\) particles. Hence the answer is option (D), tritium.
authoredSolutions.48: Phenyl methanamine (benzylamine, \(C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}NH_{2}\)) has the nitrogen lone pair insulated from the ring by an \(sp^{3}\) carbon, so it behaves like an aliphatic amine and is the strongest base. In the three anilines the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, which lowers basicity sharply, but alkyl groups on nitrogen push electron density back: \(N,N\)-dimethylaniline with two methyls is more basic than \(N\)-methylaniline with one, which is more basic than aniline itself. The order is therefore benzylamine > \(N,N\)-dimethylaniline > \(N\)-methylaniline > aniline, i.e. \(A > B > C > D\). This is option (D).
authoredSolutions.49: The ketone drawn is \(4\)-ethylhexan-3-one, \((CH_{3}CH_{2})_{2}CH-CO-CH_{2}CH_{3}\). Zn-Hg/HCl (Clemmensen reduction) converts the \(C=O\) group into \(CH_{2}\), giving the alkane \(3\)-ethylhexane, \(C_{8}H_{18}\). Passing this over \(Cr_{2}O_{3}\) at \(773\ K\) and \(10-20\) atm causes catalytic reforming: the six-carbon chain cyclises and then aromatises with loss of hydrogen, leaving the two-carbon branch as a side chain. The product is ethylbenzene, \(C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}CH_{3}\), which is option (C); \(o\)-xylene would require a \(2,3\)-dimethyl skeleton and propylbenzene would need nine carbons.
authoredSolutions.50: Seliwanoff's reagent (resorcinol in concentrated HCl) gives a rapid cherry-red colour with ketoses such as fructose, because ketoses dehydrate to furfural derivatives much faster than aldoses do. The xanthoproteic test uses concentrated \(HNO_{3}\) to nitrate the aromatic rings of tyrosine, tryptophan and phenylalanine residues, giving a yellow colour that turns orange with alkali, and so detects proteins. The two tests therefore identify ketoses and proteins respectively. Hence the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.51: The solution contains \(70.0\ mg\) of \(Na^{+}\) per \(mL\), so \(50\ mL\) contains \(70.0 \times 50 = 3500\ mg = 3.5\ g\) of \(Na^{+}\). Moles of \(Na^{+} = 3.5/23 = 0.152\ mol\), and since \(NaNO_{3}\) supplies one \(Na^{+}\) each, the same number of moles of \(NaNO_{3}\) is needed. Its molar mass is \(23 + 14 + 48 = 85\ g\ mol^{-1}\), so the mass required is \(0.152 \times 85 = 12.93\ g\). Rounded to the nearest integer this is \(13\ g\).
authoredSolutions.52: The complex is of the type \([M(AA)_{2}XY]\), with two symmetrical bidentate oxalates plus two different monodentate ligands on an octahedral \(Co(III)\) centre. Such a complex has two geometrical arrangements: one in which \(Br^{-}\) and \(NH_{3}\) are cis and one in which they are trans. The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive, but the cis isomer lacks any improper axis and exists as a non-superimposable pair of enantiomers. Counting the trans form plus the two cis enantiomers gives \(3\) stereoisomers in all.
authoredSolutions.53: The average bond energy is the enthalpy needed to atomise the molecule divided by the number of bonds, so consider \(SF_{6}(g) \rightarrow S(g) + 6F(g)\). By Hess's law \(\Delta H = \Delta H_{f}^{\circ}[S(g)] + 6\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}[F(g)] - \Delta H_{f}^{\circ}[SF_{6}(g)] = 275 + 6(80) - (-1100)\). This gives \(275 + 480 + 1100 = 1855\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\) for breaking all six \(S-F\) bonds. Dividing by \(6\) gives \(309.17\), so the average \(S-F\) bond energy is \(309\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\).
authoredSolutions.54: The cell reaction is \(Zn(s) + 2Ag^{+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2Ag(s)\) with \(n = 2\), and \(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56\ V\). The reaction quotient is \(Q = [Zn^{2+}]/[Ag^{+}]^{2} = 0.1/(0.01)^{2} = 10^{3}\). The Nernst equation gives \(E = 1.56 - \frac{0.059}{2}\log(10^{3}) = 1.56 - 0.0885 = 1.4715\ V\). Writing this as \(x \times 10^{-2}\ V\) gives \(x = 147.15\), i.e. \(147\) to the nearest integer.
authoredSolutions.55: With \(m = 10\ g = 10^{-2}\ kg\) and \(v = 90\ m\ s^{-1}\), a \(5\%\) uncertainty in velocity is \(\Delta v = 90 \times 0.05 = 4.5\ m\ s^{-1}\). Heisenberg's uncertainty principle gives \(\Delta x \geq \frac{h}{4\pi m \Delta v}\). Substituting, \(\Delta x \geq \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{4\pi \times 10^{-2} \times 4.5} = 1.17 \times 10^{-33}\ m\). Comparing with \(x \times 10^{-33}\ m\) gives \(x = 1.17\), i.e. \(1\) to the nearest integer, illustrating how negligible the positional uncertainty is for a macroscopic body.
authoredSolutions.56: In mildly alkaline (or neutral) medium permanganate is reduced to \(MnO_{2}\) and oxidises thiosulphate completely, not merely to tetrathionate as iodine does. The reaction is \(8MnO_{4}^{-} + 3S_{2}O_{3}^{2-} + H_{2}O \rightarrow 8MnO_{2} + 6SO_{4}^{2-} + 2OH^{-}\), so the product \(A\) is the sulphate ion. In \(SO_{4}^{2-}\), letting the oxidation number of sulphur be \(y\) gives \(y + 4(-2) = -2\), hence \(y = +6\). The oxidation state of sulphur in \(A\) is therefore \(6\).
authoredSolutions.57: The molality is \(m = \frac{12.2/122}{0.100} = 1.0\ mol\ kg^{-1}\), so without association the expected depression would be \(\Delta T_{f} = K_{f}m = 1.86\ K\). The observed depression is only \(0.93\ K\), so the van't Hoff factor is \(i = 0.93/1.86 = 0.5\). For complete association of \(n\) molecules into one aggregate, \(i = 1/n\), hence \(1/n = 0.5\). Therefore \(n = 2\), which is the familiar hydrogen-bonded benzoic acid dimer.
authoredSolutions.58: From the Arrhenius/Boltzmann distribution, the fraction of molecules possessing at least the activation energy is \(e^{-E_{a}/RT}\). Equating this to \(e^{-x}\) gives \(x = E_{a}/RT\). Substituting \(E_{a} = 80.9 \times 10^{3}\ J\ mol^{-1}\), \(R = 8.31\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}\) and \(T = 700\ K\) gives \(x = \frac{80900}{8.31 \times 700} = \frac{80900}{5817} = 13.91\). Rounded to the nearest integer, \(x = 14\).
authoredSolutions.59: Ammonium phosphate, \((NH_{4})_{3}PO_{4}\), is a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, so both the cation and the anion hydrolyse and the pH depends only on the relative strengths of the two parents. The standard result is \(pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_{a} - pK_{b})\), equivalently \(pH = pK_{a} + \frac{1}{2}(pK_{w} - pK_{a} - pK_{b})\). Substituting \(pK_{a} = 5.23\) and \(pK_{b} = 4.75\) gives \(pH = 5.23 + \frac{1}{2}(14 - 5.23 - 4.75) = 5.23 + 2.01 = 7.24\). To the nearest integer the pH is \(7\), i.e. very nearly neutral because the acid and base are of comparable strength.
authoredSolutions.60: In any close-packed arrangement the octahedral voids sit at the body centre and at the midpoints of the edges of the unit cell. For a face-centred cubic lattice this gives \(1 + 12 \times \frac{1}{4} = 4\) octahedral voids against \(4\) lattice points per unit cell. The count of octahedral voids therefore always equals the number of lattice sites, whatever the close-packed lattice. The number of octahedral voids per lattice site is thus \(1\).
authoredSolutions.83: \(\sigma^{2}=1\Rightarrow\sum(X_{i}-\bar X)^{2}=18\). From \(\sum(X_{i}-\alpha)=36\), \(\bar X=\alpha+2\). Then \(\sum(X_{i}-\beta)^{2}=\sum(X_{i}-\bar X)^{2}+18(\bar X-\beta)^{2}=18+18(\bar X-\beta)^{2}=90\), so \((\bar X-\beta)^{2}=4\). As \(\alpha,\beta\) are distinct, \(\beta=\bar X+2=\alpha+4\), giving \(|\alpha-\beta|=4\).
